catalog_quote: Like most Bantu languages, Fwe is a tone language: the relative pitch at which a vowel is articulated is phonologically contrastive. This is illustrated by tonal minimal pairs in (1–3), words that are identical on the segmental level, but have different tones and a different meaning. ... [sec. 2.3.4] Fwe also makes use of a second type of predictable vowel lengthening, which targets the penultimate mora of a phrase-final word. The automatic lengthening of phrase-final penultimate vowels is common in Bantu languages, and had already been noted for Fwe by Bostoen (2009: 111). ... Lengthening targets the penultimate mora of an utterance-final word ... Penultimate lengthening targets the mora, and not the syllable ... Impressionistically, penultimate lengthening is quite subtle, with only a very small difference between vowels with and without penultimate lengthening. ... [sec. 3.1.4] There…

tone_statements.quote: 2.2 Meeussen’s Rule: HH > HL /ku-zí-bátura/ > kù-zí-bàtùrà ‘to separate them’ 2.3 H retraction H in the last syllable of a clause-final word shifts to the preceding mora: /mu-ndaré/ > mùndárè ‘maize’ ... 2.4 H>F Underlying H in the last or penultimate syllable of a clause-final word becomes F: /ʒúβa/ > ʒûβà ‘day’ ... 3 Verb tone (1) Infinitive verbs Verb stem H-toned verb roots toneless verb roots ... Neutralization of stem tone contrast in many inflections, e.g. present tense ... 3.1 Melodic tone pattern 1: a high tone on the last mora of the verb
tone_statements.summary: H-toned vs toneless roots (privative H); surface L and F derived by rule (Meeussen HH>HL, H retraction to preceding mora, H>F clause-finally); four melodic H patterns by TAM; no count; one ! mark.

tone_statements.quote: Fwe has two tones, H and ø, realized as H, L, F or !H. ... Tone assignment 1. Lexical tones 2. Grammatical tones 3. Melodic tones pattern 1: melodic H on the last mora of the verb pattern 2: melodic H on the second mora of the verb stem pattern 3: melodic H on the subject concord 4. Tone rules 1. Meeussen’s Rule 2. H > F 3. H retraction ... 4. Downstep:HH > H!H ... Downstep applies to H’s on adjacent syllables, even when separated by a low-toned mora ... 5. H spread: LLL…H > HHH…H
tone_statements.locator: p. 3, 'Tone in Fwe' and 'Tone assignment'; '4. Downstep:HH > H!H' heading p. 5; 'Downstep applies to H's on adjacent syllables..' and '5. H spread' p. 7
tone_statements.summary: H vs toneless contrast; L, F, !H are surface outputs of rules. Rules refer to moras but no TBU statement. Downstep HH>H!H called phonetic; floating-L analysis declined; melodic H is grammatical.

audit.reasoning: The record rests on a 2022 open-access Language Science Press reference grammar (548 pp) with dedicated segmental-phonology and tone chapters by the language's principal fieldworker; we hold the full PDF and text, and every deciding quotation was found verbatim at the stated pages (pp. 39-40, 73, 82). The grammar describes Fwe as a tone language (H vs toneless, mora TBU) with only phrase-level positional prosody (subtle penultimate-mora lengthening of the utterance-final word, phrase-final H retraction and falling realization) and never posits word stress or accent, matching classification tonal, domain=phrase. Glottolog's four descriptive refs contain nothing better (2018 thesis = earlier version of same work; Bostoen 2009 diachronic article; Pretorius 1975 ethnography), and the author's publication list shows no separate prosody/instrumental study. sources.citation: Bostoen, Koen. 2009. Shanjo and Fwe as part of Bantu Botatwe: A diachronic phonological approach. In Akinloye Ojo & Lioba Moshi (eds.), Selected Proceedings of the 39th Annual Conference on African Linguistics, 110-130. Somerville, MA: Cascadilla Proceedings Project.
sources.quote: p. 111: 'Shanjo and Fwe have an identical 5 vowel system ... without distinctive vowel length, but with automatic penultimate vowel lengthening in citation forms or phrase-finally.' ... 'The tone systems of Shanjo and Fwe have not been studied in detail yet ... The basic tones in both languages are high and low, but high can be realized falling on the penultimate syllable of words in isolation or in phrase-final position.' Sec. 3.11: 'both languages manifest automatic penultimate vowel lengthening (27b), another common eastern Bantu phenomenon (Hyman 2003).' No stress or accent posited.
sources.note: The only other phonological description of Fwe and the source Gunnink cites (2009: 111) for phrase-final penultimate lengthening; downloaded now, it independently confirms H/L tone plus automatic phrase-final penult lengthening with no stress.
